items.stem: Which statement describes what a wave transfers?
options: Neither matter nor energy, only momentum
items.answer: Energy, without transferring matter
items.markingKey: A wave transfers energy from one place to another; the particles of the medium only oscillate about fixed positions.

items.stem: A cork floats on a pond as ripples pass it. Explain why the cork bobs up and down but does not move towards the bank.
items.answer: Water waves are transverse and transfer energy, not water; the water (and cork) only oscillates up and down about a fixed position.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: wave transfers energy not matter; 1 mark: water/cork oscillates about a fixed position (perpendicular to wave travel).

items.stem: Explain the difference between a transverse and a longitudinal wave, giving one example of each.
items.answer: Transverse: vibrations at right angles to energy transfer (e.g. light, water ripples). Longitudinal: vibrations parallel to energy transfer (e.g. sound).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each for the two directions; 1 mark for one correct example of each.

items.stem: A wave has a frequency of 5.00 Hz. Calculate its period, giving the unit.
A wave has a frequency of 125 Hz. Calculate its period, giving the unit.

A student sets up a ripple tank with a vibrating bar. The water waves have a frequency of 0.250 Hz and a wavelength of 6.00 m. (a) Calculate the period of the waves. (b) The frequency is doubled but the medium is unchanged. State the new wavelength and explain.
items.answer: (a) 4.00 s (b) 3.00 m: speed is fixed by the medium, so λ halves.
items.markingKey: (a) T = 1/f = 4.00 s [2] (b) 1 mark value; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: In a transverse wave, how do the particles of the medium vibrate?
options: They do not vibrate at all
In circles around the direction of travel
At right angles to the direction of energy transfer
Parallel to the direction of energy transfer
items.answer: At right angles to the direction of energy transfer
items.markingKey: Transverse: oscillation perpendicular to the direction of travel of the wave (e.g. light, water ripples).

items.stem: Explain why sound cannot travel through a vacuum but light can.
items.answer: Sound is a mechanical wave that needs particles to pass vibrations along; light is an electromagnetic wave that needs no medium.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: sound needs a medium (particles to vibrate); 1 mark: light is EM, does not need a medium.

items.stem: A slinky spring is pushed and pulled along its length. Describe the wave produced and how its compressions move.
items.answer: A longitudinal wave: coils oscillate along the length; compressions and rarefactions travel along the spring while each coil returns to its rest position.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: longitudinal; 1 mark: compressions/rarefactions move along, coils oscillate about rest positions.

items.stem: Two waves travel along the same ripple tank at the same speed. Wave P has frequency 25 Hz and wave Q has frequency 2 Hz. Without calculating, state which wave has the longer wavelength and explain why.
items.answer: Wave Q (the lower frequency). Since v = fλ and v is the same, λ is inversely proportional to f.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct wave; 1 mark: same speed so λ ∝ 1/f (v = fλ).

items.stem: In a ripple tank, 36 waves pass a point in 6 s. A student measures the distance across 5 neighbouring crests as 1.80 m. Calculate (a) the frequency, (b) the wavelength and (c) the speed of the waves.
items.markingKey: (a) f = 36/6 = 6.00 Hz; (b) 5 crests span 4 wavelengths so λ = 1.80/4 = 0.450 m; (c) v = fλ = 6.00 × 0.450 = 2.70 m/s. Common error: dividing by 5.

items.stem: In a ripple tank, 60 waves pass a point in 4 s. A student measures the distance across 5 neighbouring crests as 1.20 m. Calculate (a) the frequency, (b) the wavelength and (c) the speed of the waves.
items.markingKey: (a) f = 60/4 = 15.0 Hz; (b) 5 crests span 4 wavelengths so λ = 1.20/4 = 0.300 m; (c) v = fλ = 15.0 × 0.300 = 4.50 m/s. Common error: dividing by 5.

items.stem: A long slinky spring on a bench is pushed back and forth at one end. The longitudinal waves on the spring have a frequency of 0.500 Hz and a wavelength of 6.00 m. (a) Calculate the period of the waves. (b) Calculate how many waves pass a fixed point in 20 s. (c) The frequency is doubled but the medium is unchanged. State the new wavelength and explain.
items.answer: (a) 2.00 s (b) 10.0 (c) 3.00 m: speed is fixed by the medium, so λ halves.
items.markingKey: (a) T = 1/f = 2.00 s [2] (b) number = f × t = 0.500 × 20 = 10.0 [1] (c) 1 mark value; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Which equation links wave speed v, frequency f and wavelength λ?
items.answer: v = fλ
items.markingKey: Wave equation: speed = frequency × wavelength.

items.stem: Sipho says: "If I make a sound of frequency 1600 Hz instead of 800 Hz, it will travel twice as fast because v = fλ." Explain why this is wrong.
items.answer: Wave speed depends on the medium, not on the frequency. Doubling f halves λ, so v stays the same.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: speed set by medium; 1 mark: λ halves so fλ is unchanged.

items.stem: Mohammed says: "If I make a sound of frequency 400 Hz instead of 200 Hz, it will travel twice as fast because v = fλ." Explain why this is wrong.
items.answer: Wave speed depends on the medium, not on the frequency. Doubling f halves λ, so v stays the same.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: speed set by medium; 1 mark: λ halves so fλ is unchanged.

items.stem: A wave travels at 40.0 m/s with a frequency of 200 Hz. Calculate its wavelength.
items.markingKey: λ = v/f = 40.0/200 = 0.200 m. (1 mark equation/substitution, 1 mark answer with unit)

items.stem: A wave has frequency 440 Hz and wavelength 0.0450 m. Calculate its speed.
items.markingKey: v = fλ = 440 × 0.0450 = 19.8 m/s. (1 mark equation/substitution, 1 mark answer with unit)

items.stem: A wave travels at 15.0 m/s with a frequency of 440 Hz. Calculate its wavelength.
items.markingKey: λ = v/f = 15.0/440 = 0.0340 m. (1 mark equation/substitution, 1 mark answer with unit)

items.stem: A ripple tank vibrator runs at 5 Hz. In the deep region the wavelength is 3.00 cm. The waves cross into a shallow region where their speed falls to 0.0900 m/s. (a) Calculate the speed in the deep region. (b) Calculate the wavelength in the shallow region. (c) Explain what happens to the direction of the waves if they meet the boundary at an angle.
items.answer: (a) 0.150 m/s (b) 1.80 cm (c) They refract towards the normal because they slow down.
items.markingKey: (a) v = fλ = 5 × 0.0300 = 0.150 m/s [2]; (b) f unchanged = 5 Hz, λ = 0.0900/5 = 0.0180 m = 1.80 cm [2]; (c) wave slows, bends towards the normal [1].

items.stem: A ripple tank vibrator runs at 4 Hz. In the deep region the wavelength is 4.00 cm. The waves cross into a shallow region where their speed falls to 0.0960 m/s. (a) Calculate the speed in the deep region. (b) Calculate the wavelength in the shallow region. (c) Explain what happens to the direction of the waves if they meet the boundary at an angle.
items.answer: (a) 0.160 m/s (b) 2.40 cm (c) They refract towards the normal because they slow down.
items.markingKey: (a) v = fλ = 4 × 0.0400 = 0.160 m/s [2]; (b) f unchanged = 4 Hz, λ = 0.0960/4 = 0.0240 m = 2.40 cm [2]; (c) wave slows, bends towards the normal [1].

items.stem: If the frequency of a wave doubles and its speed stays the same, what happens to its wavelength?
items.answer: It halves
items.markingKey: v = fλ with v constant, so λ ∝ 1/f; doubling f halves λ.

items.stem: Mei says: "If I make a sound of frequency 2000 Hz instead of 1000 Hz, it will travel twice as fast because v = fλ." Explain why this is wrong.
items.answer: Wave speed depends on the medium, not on the frequency. Doubling f halves λ, so v stays the same.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: speed set by medium; 1 mark: λ halves so fλ is unchanged.

items.stem: Lucas says: "If I make a sound of frequency 800 Hz instead of 400 Hz, it will travel twice as fast because v = fλ." Explain why this is wrong.
items.answer: Wave speed depends on the medium, not on the frequency. Doubling f halves λ, so v stays the same.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: speed set by medium; 1 mark: λ halves so fλ is unchanged.

items.stem: Kwame says: "If I make a sound of frequency 1000 Hz instead of 500 Hz, it will travel twice as fast because v = fλ." Explain why this is wrong.
items.answer: Wave speed depends on the medium, not on the frequency. Doubling f halves λ, so v stays the same.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: speed set by medium; 1 mark: λ halves so fλ is unchanged.

items.stem: Two waves travel along the same rope at the same speed. Wave P has frequency 25 Hz and wave Q has frequency 4 Hz. Without calculating, state which wave has the longer wavelength and explain why.
items.answer: Wave Q (the lower frequency). Since v = fλ and v is the same, λ is inversely proportional to f.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct wave; 1 mark: same speed so λ ∝ 1/f (v = fλ).

items.stem: A wave has frequency 20.0 Hz and wavelength 0.400 m. Calculate its speed.
items.markingKey: v = fλ = 20.0 × 0.400 = 8.00 m/s. (1 mark equation/substitution, 1 mark answer with unit)

items.stem: A wave has frequency 25.0 Hz and wavelength 0.500 m. Calculate its speed.
items.markingKey: v = fλ = 25.0 × 0.500 = 12.5 m/s. (1 mark equation/substitution, 1 mark answer with unit)

items.stem: A loudspeaker produces sound of frequency 1.50 kHz in air, where sound travels at 340 m/s. Calculate the wavelength in cm.
items.markingKey: f = 1.50 × 10³ Hz; λ = v/f = 340/1500 = 0.227 m = 22.7 cm. Unit conversion kHz → Hz is the usual error.

items.stem: A wave travels at 0.425 m/s with a frequency of 12.5 Hz. Calculate its wavelength.
items.markingKey: λ = v/f = 0.425/12.5 = 0.0340 m. (1 mark equation/substitution, 1 mark answer with unit)

items.stem: A rope tied to a wall is shaken up and down steadily by a student. The waves on the rope have a frequency of 0.500 Hz and a wavelength of 6.00 m. (a) Calculate the time for a wave to travel 60.0 m. (b) The frequency is doubled but the medium is unchanged. State the new wavelength and explain.
items.answer: (a) 20 s (b) 3.00 m: speed is fixed by the medium, so λ halves.
items.markingKey: (a) t = d/v = 60.0/3.00 = 20 s [2] (b) 1 mark value; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: A long slinky spring on a bench is pushed back and forth at one end. The longitudinal waves on the spring have a frequency of 20.0 Hz and a wavelength of 0.0400 m. (a) The frequency is doubled but the medium is unchanged. State the new wavelength and explain. (b) State whether the longitudinal waves on the spring are transverse or longitudinal and describe the motion of the particles.
items.answer: (a) 0.0200 m: speed is fixed by the medium, so λ halves. (b) Longitudinal: particles oscillate parallel to the direction of travel.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark value; 1 mark reason [2] (b) 1 mark type; 1 mark direction of oscillation [2]

items.stem: What happens to the wavelength of water waves when they diffract through a gap?
items.answer: It stays the same
items.markingKey: Diffraction changes the direction/spreading, not the speed, frequency or wavelength.

items.stem: Explain why you can hear someone talking in the next room through an open doorway even though you cannot see them.
items.answer: Sound wavelengths (about 0.3 m to 3 m) are similar to the width of a doorway so sound diffracts strongly; light wavelengths are far smaller, so light hardly diffracts.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: diffraction of sound; 1 mark: comparison of wavelength with gap size for sound vs light.

items.stem: Explain why long-wave radio signals can be received behind hills but signals of much shorter wavelength often cannot.
items.answer: Long-wave radio has wavelengths comparable to the size of hills, so it diffracts around them; short wavelengths diffract very little.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: diffraction around obstacles; 1 mark: long λ diffracts more.

items.stem: Water waves of wavelength 1.50 cm approach two gaps: gap A is 1.50 cm wide and gap B is 12.0 cm wide. Sketch-describe the wavefronts beyond each gap and state which shows more diffraction.
items.answer: Gap A: wavefronts spread out as near-semicircles; gap B: wavefronts mostly straight with slight curving at the edges. Gap A shows more diffraction; wavelength unchanged in both.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: A spreads (curved); 1 mark: B mainly straight; 1 mark: same wavelength drawn/stated.

items.stem: Water waves of wavelength 2.50 cm approach two gaps: gap A is 2.50 cm wide and gap B is 25.0 cm wide. Sketch-describe the wavefronts beyond each gap and state which shows more diffraction.
items.answer: Gap A: wavefronts spread out as near-semicircles; gap B: wavefronts mostly straight with slight curving at the edges. Gap A shows more diffraction; wavelength unchanged in both.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: A spreads (curved); 1 mark: B mainly straight; 1 mark: same wavelength drawn/stated.

items.stem: Engineers in Nairobi are designing a harbour where incoming ocean waves have a wavelength of about 12 m. Two entrance widths are proposed: 12 m and 72 m. Using ideas about diffraction, evaluate which entrance would give calmer water for boats moored to one side of the entrance.
items.answer: The 72 m entrance: when the gap is much larger than λ the waves diffract little, so less wave energy spreads to the sides. A 12 m gap would spread waves widely into the harbour (though it lets in less energy overall).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: diffraction greatest when gap ≈ λ; 1 mark: wide gap gives little spreading to the side; 1 mark: balanced point (narrow gap admits less energy but spreads it); 1 mark: clear conclusion.

items.stem: Describe how wavefronts change when plane waves pass through a gap much wider than their wavelength.
items.answer: They pass straight through with only slight curving at the edges; the wavelength is unchanged.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: little spreading (edges only); 1 mark: same wavelength.

items.stem: Explain why the wavefronts get closer together when water waves move into a shallow region.
items.answer: The waves slow down but the frequency stays the same, so λ = v/f decreases.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: speed decreases; 1 mark: f constant so λ decreases.

items.stem: A harbour wall has a narrow entrance. Explain why boats moored just inside the wall, out of line with the entrance, still rock.
items.answer: Waves diffract as they pass through the entrance and spread into the region behind the wall.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: diffraction at gap; 1 mark: spreading reaches the shadow region.

items.stem: Plane water waves strike a straight barrier. The wavefronts make an angle of 20° with the barrier. State the angle of incidence (from the normal) and the angle that the reflected wavefronts make with the barrier.
items.answer: Angle of incidence = 20°; reflected wavefronts also make 20° with the barrier.
items.markingKey: The angle between wavefront and barrier equals the angle between ray and normal, so i = 20° [1]; i = r so reflected wavefronts at 20° [1].

items.stem: Plane water waves strike a straight barrier. The wavefronts make an angle of 60° with the barrier. State the angle of incidence (from the normal) and the angle that the reflected wavefronts make with the barrier.
items.answer: Angle of incidence = 60°; reflected wavefronts also make 60° with the barrier.
items.markingKey: The angle between wavefront and barrier equals the angle between ray and normal, so i = 60° [1]; i = r so reflected wavefronts at 60° [1].

items.stem: Plane waves of frequency 15 Hz and wavelength 4.00 cm travel across a ripple tank and pass over a sheet of glass that makes the water shallower; their speed there is 0.480 m/s. (a) Calculate the wavelength in the shallow water. (b) Describe what happens to the direction of waves that meet the boundary at an angle, and explain why.
items.answer: (a) 3.20 cm (b) They bend towards the normal (refract) because they slow down.
items.markingKey: (a) f unchanged; λ = v/f = 0.480/15 = 0.0320 m [2] (b) 1 mark direction; 1 mark slowing [2]

items.stem: Plane waves of frequency 4 Hz and wavelength 1.50 cm travel across a ripple tank and pass over a sheet of glass that makes the water shallower; their speed there is 0.0300 m/s. (a) Calculate the speed in the deep water. (b) Calculate the wavelength in the shallow water. (c) Describe what happens to the direction of waves that meet the boundary at an angle, and explain why.
items.answer: (a) 0.0600 m/s (b) 0.750 cm (c) They bend towards the normal (refract) because they slow down.
items.markingKey: (a) v = fλ = 4 × 0.0150 = 0.0600 m/s [2] (b) f unchanged; λ = v/f = 0.0300/4 = 0.00750 m [2] (c) 1 mark direction; 1 mark slowing [2]

items.stem: Diffraction is greatest when the gap width is
options: about the same as the wavelength
items.answer: about the same as the wavelength
items.markingKey: Spreading is most noticeable when gap ≈ λ.

items.stem: When a plane water wave reflects off a straight barrier, which is true?
options: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection
items.answer: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection
items.markingKey: Law of reflection: i = r, measured from the normal; λ and f are unchanged.

items.stem: A model harbour is built in a ripple tank. Waves are produced at 10 Hz with wavelength 2.00 cm in deep water and slow to 0.120 m/s near the model beach. (a) State which quantity does not change as the waves cross into shallow water. (b) Describe what happens to the direction of waves that meet the boundary at an angle, and explain why.
items.answer: (a) Frequency (b) They bend towards the normal (refract) because they slow down.
items.markingKey: (a) frequency set by source [1] (b) 1 mark direction; 1 mark slowing [2]

items.stem: Why do water waves refract when they enter shallower water?
items.answer: Their speed changes
items.markingKey: Waves slow down in shallow water; the change of speed at an angle changes direction.

items.stem: Water waves of wavelength 1.00 cm approach two gaps: gap A is 1.20 cm wide and gap B is 5.00 cm wide. Sketch-describe the wavefronts beyond each gap and state which shows more diffraction.

items.stem: A model harbour is built in a ripple tank. Waves are produced at 8 Hz with wavelength 2.50 cm in deep water and slow to 0.100 m/s near the model beach. (a) Calculate the speed in the deep water. (b) State which quantity does not change as the waves cross into shallow water.

items.answer: (a) 2.10 cm (b) Little spreading, mainly straight wavefronts with curved edges (gap ≫ λ).
items.markingKey: (a) f unchanged; λ = v/f = 0.210/10 = 0.0210 m [2] (b) 1 mark pattern linked to gap/λ; 1 mark wavelength unchanged [2]

items.stem: Which of these is a longitudinal wave?
items.answer: Sound wave in air
items.markingKey: Sound is longitudinal: the air particles oscillate parallel to the direction of travel, forming compressions and rarefactions.

items.stem: Explain in one line why a wave with a larger amplitude carries more energy.
items.answer: The particles are displaced further from rest, so more energy is needed to produce and is carried by the oscillation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: larger displacement of particles means more energy transferred.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Describe how wavefronts change when plane waves pass through a gap much wider than their wavelength. (b) Explain why long-wave radio signals can be received behind hills but signals of much shorter wavelength often cannot.
items.answer: (a) They pass straight through with only slight curving at the edges; the wavelength is unchanged. (b) Long-wave radio has wavelengths comparable to the size of hills, so it diffracts around them; short wavelengths diffract very little.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: little spreading (edges only); 1 mark: same wavelength. (b) 1 mark: diffraction around obstacles; 1 mark: long λ diffracts more.

items.stem: Water waves of wavelength 1.00 cm approach two gaps: gap A is 1.20 cm wide and gap B is 10.0 cm wide. Sketch-describe the wavefronts beyond each gap and state which shows more diffraction.
items.answer: Gap A: wavefronts spread out as near-semicircles; gap B: wavefronts mostly straight with slight curving at the edges. Gap A shows more diffraction; wavelength unchanged in both.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: A spreads (curved); 1 mark: B mainly straight; 1 mark: same wavelength drawn/stated.

items.stem: What is the amplitude of a wave?
options: The distance from a crest to a trough
The distance from a crest to the next crest
The maximum displacement of a point from its rest position
The number of waves passing a point each second
items.answer: The maximum displacement of a point from its rest position
items.markingKey: Amplitude = maximum displacement from the undisturbed (rest) position, measured from the centre line to a crest.

items.stem: Two waves travel along the same stretched spring at the same speed. Wave P has frequency 10 Hz and wave Q has frequency 50 Hz. Without calculating, state which wave has the longer wavelength and explain why.
items.answer: Wave P (the lower frequency). Since v = fλ and v is the same, λ is inversely proportional to f.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct wave; 1 mark: same speed so λ ∝ 1/f (v = fλ).

items.stem: In a ripple tank, 36 waves pass a point in 12 s. A student measures the distance across 7 neighbouring crests as 1.80 m. Calculate (a) the frequency, (b) the wavelength and (c) the speed of the waves.
items.markingKey: (a) f = 36/12 = 3.00 Hz; (b) 7 crests span 6 wavelengths so λ = 1.80/6 = 0.300 m; (c) v = fλ = 3.00 × 0.300 = 0.900 m/s. Common error: dividing by 7.

items.stem: In a ripple tank, 12 waves pass a point in 5 s. A student measures the distance across 7 neighbouring crests as 1.80 m. Calculate (a) the frequency, (b) the wavelength and (c) the speed of the waves.
items.markingKey: (a) f = 12/5 = 2.40 Hz; (b) 7 crests span 6 wavelengths so λ = 1.80/6 = 0.300 m; (c) v = fλ = 2.40 × 0.300 = 0.720 m/s. Common error: dividing by 7.

items.stem: A fishing boat at anchor rises and falls as sea waves pass under it. The sea waves have a frequency of 0.250 Hz and a wavelength of 8.00 m. (a) Calculate the time for a wave to travel 30.0 m. (b) The frequency is doubled but the medium is unchanged. State the new wavelength and explain.
items.answer: (a) 15 s (b) 4.00 m: speed is fixed by the medium, so λ halves.
items.markingKey: (a) t = d/v = 30.0/2.00 = 15 s [2] (b) 1 mark value; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A wave passes from deep to shallow water. Which quantity stays the same? (b) Which equation links wave speed v, frequency f and wavelength λ?
items.answer: (a) Frequency (b) v = fλ
items.markingKey: (a) Frequency is set by the source and does not change on refraction; speed and wavelength both decrease in shallow water. (b) Wave equation: speed = frequency × wavelength.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why sound cannot travel through a vacuum but light can. (b) Explain in one line why a wave with a larger amplitude carries more energy.
items.answer: (a) Sound is a mechanical wave that needs particles to pass vibrations along; light is an electromagnetic wave that needs no medium. (b) The particles are displaced further from rest, so more energy is needed to produce and is carried by the oscillation.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: sound needs a medium (particles to vibrate); 1 mark: light is EM, does not need a medium. (b) 1 mark: larger displacement of particles means more energy transferred.

items.stem: Two waves travel along the same rope at the same speed. Wave P has frequency 25 Hz and wave Q has frequency 20 Hz. Without calculating, state which wave has the longer wavelength and explain why.
items.answer: Wave Q (the lower frequency). Since v = fλ and v is the same, λ is inversely proportional to f.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct wave; 1 mark: same speed so λ ∝ 1/f (v = fλ).

items.stem: A wave travels at 15.0 m/s with a frequency of 10.0 Hz. Calculate its wavelength.
items.markingKey: λ = v/f = 15.0/10.0 = 1.50 m. (1 mark equation/substitution, 1 mark answer with unit)

items.stem: A wave has frequency 20.0 Hz and wavelength 3.00 m. Calculate its speed.
items.markingKey: v = fλ = 20.0 × 3.00 = 60.0 m/s. (1 mark equation/substitution, 1 mark answer with unit)

items.stem: A student sets up a ripple tank with a vibrating bar. The water waves have a frequency of 0.200 Hz and a wavelength of 4.00 m. (a) Calculate the time for a wave to travel 8.00 m. (b) State whether the water waves are transverse or longitudinal and describe the motion of the particles.
items.answer: (a) 10 s (b) Transverse: particles oscillate perpendicular to the direction of travel.
items.markingKey: (a) t = d/v = 8.00/0.800 = 10 s [2] (b) 1 mark type; 1 mark direction of oscillation [2]

items.stem: A rope tied to a wall is shaken up and down steadily by a student. The waves on the rope have a frequency of 0.500 Hz and a wavelength of 15.0 m. (a) Calculate the speed of the waves. (b) Calculate the period of the waves. (c) The frequency is doubled but the medium is unchanged. State the new wavelength and explain.
items.answer: (a) 7.50 m/s (b) 2.00 s (c) 7.50 m: speed is fixed by the medium, so λ halves.
items.markingKey: (a) v = fλ = 0.500 × 15.0 = 7.50 m/s [2] (b) T = 1/f = 2.00 s [2] (c) 1 mark value; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Diffraction is greatest when the gap width is (b) When a plane water wave reflects off a straight barrier, which is true?
items.answer: (a) about the same as the wavelength (b) The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection
items.markingKey: (a) Spreading is most noticeable when gap ≈ λ. (b) Law of reflection: i = r, measured from the normal; λ and f are unchanged.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A harbour wall has a narrow entrance. Explain why boats moored just inside the wall, out of line with the entrance, still rock. (b) Explain why the wavefronts get closer together when water waves move into a shallow region.
items.answer: (a) Waves diffract as they pass through the entrance and spread into the region behind the wall. (b) The waves slow down but the frequency stays the same, so λ = v/f decreases.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: diffraction at gap; 1 mark: spreading reaches the shadow region. (b) 1 mark: speed decreases; 1 mark: f constant so λ decreases.

items.stem: Plane water waves strike a straight barrier. The wavefronts make an angle of 50° with the barrier. State the angle of incidence (from the normal) and the angle that the reflected wavefronts make with the barrier.
items.answer: Angle of incidence = 50°; reflected wavefronts also make 50° with the barrier.
items.markingKey: The angle between wavefront and barrier equals the angle between ray and normal, so i = 50° [1]; i = r so reflected wavefronts at 50° [1].

items.stem: Plane waves of frequency 4 Hz and wavelength 2.00 cm travel across a ripple tank and pass over a sheet of glass that makes the water shallower; their speed there is 0.0600 m/s. (a) State which quantity does not change as the waves cross into shallow water. (b) Describe what happens to the direction of waves that meet the boundary at an angle, and explain why.
items.answer: (a) Frequency (b) They bend towards the normal (refract) because they slow down.
items.markingKey: (a) frequency set by source [1] (b) 1 mark direction; 1 mark slowing [2]

items.stem: In a ripple tank the water waves have wavelength 4.00 cm in the deep part. The dipper vibrates at 8 Hz. Over a shallow region the waves move at 0.192 m/s. (a) Calculate the speed in the deep water. (b) State which quantity does not change as the waves cross into shallow water. (c) Describe what happens to the direction of waves that meet the boundary at an angle, and explain why.
items.answer: (a) 0.320 m/s (b) Frequency (c) They bend towards the normal (refract) because they slow down.
items.markingKey: (a) v = fλ = 8 × 0.0400 = 0.320 m/s [2] (b) frequency set by source [1] (c) 1 mark direction; 1 mark slowing [2]

items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: little spreading (edges only); 1 mark: same wavelength. (b) 1 mark: diffraction around obstacles; 1 mark: long λ diffracts more.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A harbour wall has a narrow entrance. Explain why boats moored just inside the wall, out of line with the entrance, still rock. (b) Explain why you can hear someone talking in the next room through an open doorway even though you cannot see them.
items.answer: (a) Waves diffract as they pass through the entrance and spread into the region behind the wall. (b) Sound wavelengths (about 0.3 m to 3 m) are similar to the width of a doorway so sound diffracts strongly; light wavelengths are far smaller, so light hardly diffracts.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: diffraction at gap; 1 mark: spreading reaches the shadow region. (b) 1 mark: diffraction of sound; 1 mark: comparison of wavelength with gap size for sound vs light.

items.answer: Gap A: wavefronts spread out as near-semicircles; gap B: wavefronts mostly straight with slight curving at the edges. Gap A shows more diffraction; wavelength unchanged in both.
